nameStory: Virginia meadowbeauty gets its name from its stunning pink flowers that brighten wet meadows and bog edges throughout much of eastern North America, including Virginia where it was first scientifically described. The alternate common name 'handsome Harry' reflects just how eye-catching this native wildflower can be when it's in full bloom.
description: Virginia meadowbeauty is a showy native wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall with bright pink, four-petaled flowers. The plant has a square stem and opposite leaves that are lance-shaped with prominent parallel veins. It forms small colonies in wet, acidic areas and blooms from mid-summer into early fall, creating splashes of vibrant color in otherwise green landscapes.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Four bright pink petals surround eight prominent yellow stamens that curve dramatically outward like tiny bananas. Each flower is about 1 inch across with a distinctive cross-shaped appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves are lance-shaped with 3-5 prominent parallel veins running from base to tip. The leaves feel slightly rough and have a distinctive ribbed texture you can feel with your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square, reddish stems that feel distinctly four-angled when rolled between your fingers. Plants often form small colonies connected by underground runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Urn-shaped seed capsules develop after flowering, splitting open at the top to release tiny seeds. The dried capsules persist into fall and rattle when shaken.

habitat: Look for Virginia meadowbeauty in wet, acidic soils of bogs, pond edges, wet meadows, and ditches throughout New England. It thrives in areas that stay moist but aren't permanently flooded, often growing alongside cranberries, pitcher plants, and sedges in acidic wetlands.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish shoots from underground runners, with the distinctive square stems and opposite leaves becoming apparent by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, with the bright pink flowers opening in succession over several weeks.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the development of urn-shaped seed capsules. Leaves may turn reddish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground runners, leaving dried stems and rattling seed capsules as the only above-ground evidence.

funFact: The eight curved yellow stamens don't just look decorative - they actually shoot pollen out like tiny cannons when bumble bees vibrate them with a technique called 'buzz pollination,' the same method bees use on tomato flowers!
confusionNotes: The four pink petals and square stem make Virginia meadowbeauty quite distinctive, but before flowering it might be confused with other wetland plants. Remember the 'square stem test' - roll the stem between your fingers to feel the four distinct angles, which most other wetland plants lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting a Virginia origin, this plant ranges much more widely across eastern North America and is actually quite at home in New England's acidic wetlands. It belongs to a largely tropical plant family, making it one of the few temperate representatives of the melastome family in our region.
compareHints: Virginia meadowbeauty can be distinguished from its close relative Maryland meadowbeauty by its habitat preferences and leaf shape. Virginia meadowbeauty prefers wetter, more consistently moist soils and has narrower, more lance-shaped leaves, while Maryland meadowbeauty tolerates drier sandy soils and has broader, more oval leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Maryland meadowbeauty differs from Virginia meadowbeauty primarily in its flower color, which tends to be paler (often white or very pale pink) compared to Virginia meadowbeauty's typically deeper pink to purple blooms.
